https://www.politico.eu/article/nigel-fa.text: LONDON — Questions are swirling around the British polling industry — and piling up for the company implicated in a Reform UK party scandal that prompted the resignation of two senior party aides. The scandal hinged on donations from undercover reporters posing as a wealthy American benefactor and his son that were used to pay for a real set of high-impact polls that were released without disclosing the funding source. These polls were carried out by the influential opinion research firm JL Partners, which has become a fixture of the British polling landscape since it was founded seven years ago by James Johnson, who served as an adviser to Theresa May when she was prime minister. Advertisement Advertisement Since the sting video first aired last week, former employees and clients of JL Partners have told POLITICO that the company carried out other polls where the funder was not declared — while similar lapses have occurred at other well-known British polling companies. Rules set out by the British Polling Council , the industry watchdog, specify that all research carried out by pollsters which enters the public domain “must include reference to the… client commissioning the survey” as well as dates, methodology and sample size. JL Partners did not respond to requests for comment on these fresh claims. The company told Channel 4 News in response to the report about their work for Reform UK last week: “Despite there being no concern about the accuracy of our work, the report did reveal weaknesses in our procedures.” The British Polling Council said in a statement about the Channel 4 News report that it was “clear there have been breaches” of the watchdog’s rules, adding: “We are seeking further information from the BPC member concerned.” Reform UK denies any wrongdoing in relation to the sting, which is now under investigation by the Met Police. Tory leadership races Johnson’s firm conducted polls on three occasions during the Tory leadership elections in 2022 and 2024 which received press coverage without disclosing who paid for them either in the media reports or in the company’s published tables. Advertisement Advertisement JL Partners conducted internal research for Rishi Sunak’s 2022 bid for the leadership and Tom Tugendhat’s 2024 campaign and Johnson had personal ties to both camps, according to two people linked to the pollster and three people linked the Conservative Party, who were granted anonymity to speak candidly. Two of these people went further, and claimed allies of the candidates had arranged polls without it ever being disclosed. These polls produced positive findings for the candidates in question and were subsequently shared with the media, the same people said. There is no suggestion the findings were manipulated. An ally of Sunak denied that his campaign had commissioned the poll in question. Tugendhat declined to comment. Rishi Sunak leaves No. 10 Downing St. in London in November 2023. | Leon Neal/Getty Images A JL Partners poll conducted in 2022, which was picked up by the Telegraph , showed Rishi Sunak was rated most highly by Tory voters asked who would make a good prime minister, but did not mention who was behind the poll. A person familiar with the Telegraph’s publication process said they didn’t have any record of being given any more information than what was published. Another survey carried out by JL Partners in 2024, covered by the Daily Express , quoted Johnson as saying it was “a good poll for Suella Braverman and Tom Tugendhat” without any mention of who commissioned it. Reach PLC declined to comment on behalf of the Express. Advertisement Advertisement A news item on BBC Radio 5Live in the same year concentrated on a focus group with broadly positive findings for Tugendhat. The focus group was commissioned by the BBC, but it is not known who paid for it. Dominic Cummings, former chief of staff to Boris Johnson, questioned the BBC Radio 5Live feature at the time, posting on X : “Pollsters should make clear when they are being paid by campaigns. And a media company that cared about honesty to their audience would insist on this.” A BBC spokesperson told POLITICO: “This focus group was commissioned by BBC Radio 5Live from JL Partners at no cost to the BBC. The BBC understood that no third party had funded or commissioned the work and the programme made clear that the focus group was not representative of wider public opinion.” Questions for industry POLITICO also discovered several instances of other pollsters failing to cite their clients. JL Partners director Johnson wrote an op-ed in the Telegraph earlier this year discussing a shift in public opinion against assisted dying without mentioning the poll cited in the piece was paid for by the Christian lobbying group CARE. Johnson, the firm’s founder, has also contributed opinion columns to POLITICO in the past, in some cases citing his polling without disclosing who paid for it. Advertisement Advertisement A recent Opinium poll carried by the website Guido Fawkes which highlighted Londoners would rather have an entrepreneur than an ex-minister as mayor did not state the poll was commissioned by London mayoral hopeful Festus Akinbusoye. While this information was included in an Evening Standard write-up of the poll, it was only published belatedly by Opinium. A spokesperson for Opinium said: “We take our responsibilities as a member of the British Polling Council seriously and are committed to meeting the requirements that apply when polling enters the public domain.” They added they had rectified the way the tables were labeled, which they said was due to an “administrative oversight.” Liberal Democrat placards are stacked against a tree in Surrey, England on March 24, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images In another case in January 2023, the Liberal Democrats commissioned Savanta to ask voters who was responsible for the problems the country faces. The respondents were asked to choose between three named Conservative prime ministers, the Conservative Party itself, and the COVID pandemic and the Ukraine war, with no other answers available. The poll was private until some of its results were briefed to the Observer newspaper , which brought it under the British Polling Council’s transparency rules. Despite this, Savanta did not upload the full tables — confirming the client, sample size and details of the questions and answers — until POLITICO contacted the firm this week. A Savanta spokesperson said the failure to upload the tables was “an oversight on our part.” Transparency campaigners have said it is time that polling firms were held to tougher standards. Tim Picton from the campaign group Spotlight on Corruption said: “These alarming revelations suggest that this is a long-standing issue that goes beyond just one polling company. It is vital that the British Polling Council now investigates these cases and assesses if there is a wider culture of polling companies working hand in glove with political parties while not declaring the relationship.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cry8.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Tensions between the TPLF and the government have been escalating this year By Teklemariam Bekit BBC Tigrinya Published 23 September 2026, 12:42 BST Updated 1 hour ago Ethiopia's government and the party in control of the northern region of Tigray have accused each other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a return to full-scale conflict. Getachew Reda, a cabinet minister and adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched offensives in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. Earlier, the Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced to enter a "defensive war". The statement followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray. The two-year war in Tigray ended in 2022 - but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating a peace deal. It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the African Union's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, announced an alliance with six other armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa. Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance Published 1 day ago "It is rather heartbreaking to learn that, despite efforts by many, including the international community, to avoid yet another round of war in Tigray, the TPLF leadership early this morning launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara," Getachew said in a statement shared on social media. The adviser to Prime Minster Abiy Ahmed previously led Tigray's interim administration, but he fell out with the TPLF in 2025 and joined the federal government. Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray. Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday. This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days. On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities. The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes starting at around 03:30. "This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said. Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools. He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces. But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun. The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not commented on the alleged strikes. On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an "open invasion" of the region, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity. It further accused the government of violating international humanitarian and human rights laws, saying public services and critical infrastructure had been disrupted. Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid. It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents. Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, the AU-brokered deal that formally ended the conflict in November 2022. In July, Prime Minister Abiy accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament. Just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy. There have also been reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Four people were arrested after drones attacked the Zawiya oil station, causing a fire. Three Libyans were arrested and have been linked to Saddam Haftar. Photograph: Mahmud Turkia/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Four people were arrested after drones attacked the Zawiya oil station, causing a fire. Three Libyans were arrested and have been linked to Saddam Haftar. Photograph: Mahmud Turkia/AFP/Getty Images Libya Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities Western Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks down Patrick Wintour Sat 3 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 05.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in western Libya have upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country. Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions. But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah. Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors. View image in fullscreen Khalifa Haftar. Photograph: Esam Omran Al-Fetori/Reuters Donald Trump’s Africa adviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister. Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.” But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces. Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation. 0:25 Libyan oil refinery engulfed in flames after drone attack – video On 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar. Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said. The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change. Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.” He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war. The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east. Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance. For thus averting World War III, Col. Petrov is reprimanded. 1950— A U.S. Navy minesweeper begins six days of spraying live bacteria into the air two miles upwind of San Francisco; 800K citizens get a dose. 1945— Mistaking him for a French officer, Viet Minh in Saigon kill OSS Lieut. Col. Peter Dewey. Days before he had filed a report saying the U.S. “ought to clear out of Southeast Asia.” 1933— The same day G-Men arrest Machine Gun Kelly, ten men escape from an Indiana prison using guns smuggled in by John Dillinger. 1918— The Battle of the Meuse-Argonne begins, the last great battle of the War to End All Wars. 1908— Józef Piłsudski, Poland’s future Chief of State, loots a Russian mail train to fund a revolution. 1901— Lincoln’s body is viewed before being covered with two tons of concrete. Among 23 present is Fleetwood Linley, 13, who lives until 1963. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has been criticised after saying that he disagreed that parliamentary debate was connected with political violence. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP View image in fullscreen The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has been criticised after saying that he disagreed that parliamentary debate was connected with political violence. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP Helen Haines Angus Taylor criticised for ‘tone deaf’ response to alleged attack on Helen Haines Zali Steggall and Monique Ryan say Coalition leader was wrong to deny link between parliamentary debate and political violence Tom McIlroy Political editor Mon 26 Oct 2026 02.41 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 03.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Angus Taylor has been criticised for his response to the alleged attack on Helen Haines , with crossbenchers Monique Ryan and Zali Steggall labelling a speech by the opposition leader “tone deaf” and saying he did not “read the room”. Parliament returned in Canberra on Monday, a week after an alleged attack outside the Indi MP’s northern Victorian electorate office, which led to her losing both legs. A 43-year-old man has been charged and the incident continues to be investigated. Former Liberal leader Peter Dutton told News24 he believed more violence against politicians was “inevitable” in Australia. Police have not revealed any established motive for the Haines attack. “It came as no surprise to me, I am sorry to say. I think it has been building for a long period of time,” he said on Monday. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here The episode has sparked debate about the safety of MPs and the state of the political environment, including the culture of parliamentary debates. The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, and the One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce have rejected calls for a change in practice to cool Australia’s political debate. “In the past week, it has been suggested by some there is a causal connection between robust parliamentary debate and political violence,” Taylor said. “I disagree with this view. AFP boss says politicians’ heated rhetoric is fuelling threats against MPs Read more “The Westminster system is about settling differences through robust and rigorous debate, not violence. “Importantly, we debate with adversarial vigour, but we never allow that vigorous parliamentary debate to spill over into violence. People who resort to intimidation and violence cross a line that must never be crossed.” He said Labor had been correct to call out far-right extremism in Australia but called for all extremism to be rejected. He said judges should “come down harder” on people found guilty of intimidation or violence. “Another thing we must do is celebrate Australia more readily. Too many Australians have been taught to feel guilty and shame about our country and about our history. “Is it any wonder that some feel deep animosity towards our democracy, our institutions, and our nation?” Joyce told News24 his thoughts and prayers remained with Haines and her family, calling the alleged attack “so unAustralian”. “Unfortunately what we’re seeing in Australia and around the world is a change in dynamics,” Joyce said. “I think parliament has got its part to play but I don’t think it’s going to be a solution to the problem. “The issues, such as the Palestinian march across the [Sydney Harbour] Bridge, the vindictive, arsenic type of rhetoric that we see in the public realm, these are all part of it. “I think it’s foolish to think if question time changes, Australia changes. Not necessarily, in fact highly unlikely.” Steggall, the independent Warringah MP, who sits next to Haines in the lower house, said she was personally disappointed by Taylor’s speech. “There is a link between our words and actions,” she said. “I did not feel that Angus Taylor read the room when it comes to the lesson that Helen would like us all to learn. Helen Haines vigil sparks calls for greater safety for women in politics – video “To make what’s happened to her, the utter tragedy of it, make sense to all of us, make sense for Australia, then we have to be able to take responsibility for the impact our words and our debate has beyond the walls of parliament.” She said the same caution should be applied to media reporting, election advertising and social media posts. Steggall referenced conversations with Haines’s husband, Phil Haines, in Canberra on Monday. “His words to us, asking us to raise the bar so that when Helen does come back to this place, there’s been a meaningful shift in how we can have a respectful debate,” she said. “We can disagree respectfully, but words matter and have an impact.” Ryan, the Kooyong independent, called Taylor’s response “tone deaf” and “hugely disappointing”. “If Angus Taylor doesn’t think that the words that we use matter, I don’t understand how he aspires to lead a political party,” she told ABC TV. “If we can’t rise to the occasion now after something as unthinkable as what happened to Helen and think about how we behave in the house and in the public space … we’re never going to do that.” Explore more on these topics Helen Haines Angus Taylor Zali Steggall Australian politics news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Australians should prepare for online services to go down unexpectedly as threats rise, cyber agency warns Helen Haines’s first words after alleged attack revealed as MPs honour her ‘empathy and grace’ Unreasonable and unfair: damning investigation criticises Labor’s algorithm-based tool for aged care Haines tribute speeches to open parliament, but Labor mustn’t overlook broader causes of boiling anger AFP boss says politicians’ heated rhetoric is fuelling threats against MPs The tragic events of the past week have shown Australians who we are – and it’s a long way from our image of ourselves Helen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attack The alleged attack on Helen Haines shocked the nation.
